Introduction to Generative Adversarial Networks"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) represent a cornerstone in unsupervised deep learning, introduced by Ian Goodfellow et al. in 2014. A GAN consists of two neural networks competing against each other in a zero-sum game framework: the Generator and the Discriminator."},{"order":4,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Generator (G): Takes a random noise vector z from a prior distribution p_z(z) and maps it to the data space, attempting to produce synthetic data that mimics the true data distribution p_data."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Discriminator (D): Acts as a binary classifier. It evaluates both real data from the training set and fake data generated by G, outputting a scalar probability representing whether the input sample is real (1) or fake (0)."},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Mathematical Formulation of Minimax Loss"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"The original GAN is framed as a minimax game with value function V(D, G). The objective is optimized through alternating gradient descent steps: maximizing the capability of D to distinguish real from fake, and simultaneously minimizing the ability of D to detect G's forgeries."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"min_G max_D V(D, G) = E_{x ~ p_data(x)}[log D(x)] + E_{z ~ p_z(z)}[log(1 - D(G(z)))]"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"3. PyTorch Implementation of Vanilla GAN Loss"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Below is a practical code snippet illustrating how the adversarial loss is calculated and optimized in PyTorch for both the discriminator and generator."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# Initialize loss function
criterion = nn.BCELoss()

# Discriminator loss calculation
# real_images: tensor from dataset, fake_images: generated by G
real_labels = torch.ones(batch_size, 1)
fake_labels = torch.zeros(batch_size, 1)

# Loss on real images
outputs_real = discriminator(real_images)
d_loss_real = criterion(outputs_real, real_labels)

# Loss on fake images
outputs_fake = discriminator(fake_images.detach())
d_loss_fake = criterion(outputs_fake, fake_labels)

# Total Discriminator Loss
d_loss = d_loss_real + d_loss_fake

# Generator loss calculation (wants D to think fake images are real)
g_outputs = discriminator(fake_images)
g_loss = criterion(g_outputs, real_labels)"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Alternative Loss Functions in Modern GANs"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"While Vanilla GANs provide a strong theoretical foundation, they suffer from training instability, vanishing gradients, and mode collapse. Consequently, alternative loss formulations have been developed."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Wasserstein GAN (WGAN): Replaces the Jensen-Shannon divergence with the Earth Mover's (Wasserstein-1) distance, providing smoother gradients and resolving vanishing gradient issues during training."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Least Squares GAN (LSGAN): Adopts the least-squares loss function for the discriminator, penalizing samples that fall far on the correct side of the decision boundary to encourage the generation of data closer to the true manifold."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Non-Saturating GAN Loss: Modifies the generator objective from minimizing log(1 - D(G(z))) to maximizing log(D(G(z))), providing stronger gradients early in training when the generator is weak."},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"5. Conclusion"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Understanding GAN losses is crucial for successful generative modeling. By balancing the minimax game between the generator and discriminator, and selecting the appropriate loss formulation (such as Wasserstein or Least Squares), practitioners can stabilize training and synthesize high-fidelity data."}]
